content: Upon initiation of treatment, moxifloxacin can be discontinued. If the treatment regimen is BPAL from the start or is switched to BPAL, the total duration can be extended to 39 weeks, starting from the initiation of BPALM/BPAL therapy. This extension is warranted in cases where sputum culture conversion fails between months 4 and 6 of treatment or based on the clinical judgment of the treating physician. If doses are missed, up to one month can be added to the overall treatment duration to compensate for the missed doses. The GDG panel recognized minor differences in treatment durations between BPALM and BPAL regimens as studied in two trials. They recommended standardizing the BPALM treatment duration to 6 months (26 weeks) during programmatic implementation. For BPAL, they suggested the possibility of extending the duration to 9 months (39 weeks) if sputum cultures remain positive between months 4 and 6. All medications in the regimen should be used throughout the treatment duration, including any potential extension from 26 to 39 weeks when BPAL is used. Ideally, missing doses of all drugs in the regimen should be avoided. However, if doses are missed, interruptions longer than 7 days should be compensated by extending the treatment duration to ensure 26 or 39 weeks of prescribed doses are completed within an overall period of 7 or 10 months, respectively. The TB-PRACTECAL and ZeNix trials employed different tolerances for treatment interruptions and missing doses, with the ZeNix trial providing specific rules for linezolid administration. The GDG panel suggested standardizing the allowable missing doses and the approach to linezolid administration. A pragmatic approach was recommended to guide clinical judgment and address minor deviations in individual cases: 1. Efforts should be made to support the patient and manage adverse events to ensure uninterrupted treatment and adherence to all medications in the regimen. If a medication cannot be tolerated, it should be stopped. 2. Consecutive treatment interruptions of up to 2 weeks for all medications in the regimen should be compensated by extending the treatment duration. 3. Non-consecutive missed doses of all medications in the regimen, up to a cumulative total of 4 weeks, should also be compensated by extending the treatment duration. 4. After at least 9 weeks of consecutive administration of linezolid at the recommended dose (600 mg daily), if intolerability occurs, the dose can be reduced to 300 mg daily or omitted entirely (while continuing other medications in the regimen) for a maximum of 8 weeks throughout the treatment course. If any of these tolerances are exceeded, a thorough assessment of the patient’s status is required to decide whether to continue or modify the treatment strategy. Patients receiving BPALM/BPAL regimens should undergo baseline testing and be monitored during treatment using relevant clinical and laboratory testing schedules. If feasible, follow-up 12 months after treatment completion is recommended to monitor for relapse, including sputum culture and smear testing. The bacteriological status of the patient should be confirmed before treatment initiation, with confirmation of TB disease and rifampicin resistance as a minimum. Monthly sputum cultures are recommended for patients with MDR/RR-TB during treatment. Failure to convert sputum culture at or after the fourth month of treatment may indicate a failing treatment regimen. Drug susceptibility testing (DST) for fluoroquinolones is critical to support the prescription of the appropriate BPALM or BPAL combination, maximizing efficacy and minimizing unnecessary toxicity. National programs are strongly encouraged to establish DST capacity to test for resistance to bedaquiline and linezolid at baseline, particularly in cases with fluoroquinolone resistance, and to test samples from patients without bacteriological conversion after month 4 of BPALM/BPAL treatment. Clinicians should monitor for adverse events such as fatigue, anorexia, nausea, jaundice, dark urine, liver tenderness, hepatomegaly, peripheral or optic neuropathy, and conduct laboratory tests including ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, complete blood count, and serum potassium, calcium, and magnesium (correcting abnormalities as needed). An ECG should be obtained before treatment initiation. A suggested monitoring schedule is provided in the operational handbook on DR-TB treatment. The WHO aDSM framework should be applied to all MDR-TB regimens to ensure adequate monitoring for adverse events and prompt responses, alongside monitoring for treatment outcomes, including early detection of treatment failure. Additional evidence on adverse events will be crucial to build the evidence base on the safety of new regimens in diverse settings. WHO suggests using a 9-month all-oral regimen rather than longer (18-month) regimens for patients with MDR/RR-TB without fluoroquinolone resistance. This conditional recommendation is based on very low certainty of evidence. The 9-month regimen includes bedaquiline (used for 6 months) combined with levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, ethionamide, ethambutol, high-dose isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and clofazimine (for 4 months, extendable to 6 months if the patient remains sputum smear-positive at the end of 4 months), followed by levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, clofazimine, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide (for 5 months). Ethionamide can be replaced by 2 months of linezolid (600 mg daily). This regimen may also be used in pregnant women, unlike the ethionamide-containing regimen. This recommendation applies to individuals with MDR/RR-TB without fluoroquinolone resistance, patients without extensive TB disease or severe extrapulmonary TB, those with less than 1 month of prior exposure to bedaquiline, fluoroquinolones, ethionamide, linezolid, and clofazimine (or with resistance to these drugs ruled out), individuals regardless of HIV status, and children or other age groups with a high likelihood of MDR/RR-TB based on clinical signs and history of contact with confirmed MDR/RR-TB cases. The rationale for this recommendation is based on evidence showing that 9-month regimens are preferred over longer regimens for eligible patients. Extensive pulmonary TB is defined as bilateral cavitary disease or extensive parenchymal damage on chest radiography. Severe extrapulmonary TB includes miliary TB or TB meningitis. In children under 15 years, advanced disease is usually defined by the presence of cavities or bilateral disease on chest radiography, and severe extrapulmonary forms exclude isolated lymphadenopathy. The assessments compared the outcomes of the 9-month regimen with linezolid for 2 months versus the same regimen with ethionamide for 4 months, as well as the 9-month regimen with linezolid versus longer regimens including bedaquiline and linezolid. Data from South Africa showed that the 9-month regimen with linezolid can be recommended as an alternative to the ethionamide-containing regimen and both are preferable to longer regimens for eligible patients. However, these recommendations do not extend to patients with extensive TB disease or severe extrapulmonary TB.
